title: The dove and the olive leaf (Genesis 8)
hook: the waters go down, and the dove comes back with a fresh leaf

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ark, a tevah, a box with no sail that kept life afloat on dark water.

Months pass inside the ark. Then the turn, in four words: "And God remembered Noah." A wind passes over the earth, and slowly the water goes down. The ark settles on the mountains of Ararat. Noah opens the window and sends out a raven; it flies back and forth and never really comes home. Then a dove. She finds nowhere to rest her foot, and comes back, and Noah reaches out his hand and brings her in. He waits seven days and sends her again. And that evening she comes back with something in her beak.
screen: `AND GOD REMEMBERED NOAH.` → `A RAVEN, THEN A DOVE.` → `SHE COMES BACK IN THE EVENING.`

segments.voice: In the old JPS translation, the dove came in to him at eventide, "and lo in her mouth an olive-leaf freshly plucked." Freshly plucked: that's the whole news. Not a leaf floating on the water, left over from before, but a fresh one, torn from a living tree. Somewhere, something is growing again. So Noah knew, the Torah says, that the waters were going down. But he doesn't throw open the door. He waits another seven days and sends the dove once more, and this time she doesn't come back. Even then, he waits until God tells him to go out. The leaf isn't the end of the flood. It's the first sign the end is coming. The dove, in Hebrew, is yonah, the same name as the prophet Jonah. And the rabbis wondered why a dove would choose an olive leaf, of all things. It's bitter. The Talmud imagines her speaking: better my food be bitter as an olive and come from God's hand, than sweet as honey and depend on flesh and blood. She'd rather have something bitter and free. Over the centuries, the dove with an olive leaf became a sign of peace far beyond Jewish tradition. But the story's own meaning is quieter than peace. It's easing. Things don't snap back to normal. A leaf comes back. Then the dove doesn't. Then, at last, the door.
screen: `AN OLIVE LEAF FRESHLY PLUCKED.` · `NOAH STILL WAITS.` · `YONAH — THE DOVE.` · `BITTER, FROM GOD'S HAND.` · then, large: `THE LEAF COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: Think of something in your life that has felt like a flood: long, dark, out of your control, maybe still going. Look gently for one fresh leaf, one thing a little easier than it was: a night of better sleep, a morning without dread. If you pray, you can give thanks for it; it doesn't have to mean the flood is over.
Yonah, Hebrew for dove, the same name as the prophet Jonah. The first living sign after the flood: not the end of the waiting, but news that something is growing.
Your line: the leaf comes back. That's day thirty-four; tomorrow, a sign in the clouds: the rainbow.

howItsDone: Jews read this passage each autumn in the Torah portion Noach, and many read the Talmud's teaching about the dove's bitter olive leaf alongside it.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 8:11 ('and lo in her mouth an olive-leaf freshly plucked', hyphenation included) and 8:1.
Dove's words about bitter food from God's hand: Eruvin 18b (also Genesis Rabbah 33:6). Paraphrased; confirm.
'The dove with an olive leaf became a sign of peace far beyond Jewish tradition': general cultural claim, kept vague on purpose.
Noah waits for God's command to leave (8:15–16): confirm framing.
